Systematic sampling

Source: R/design-systematic.R
design_systematic.Rd

Walks the rows at a fixed step. Give interval to take every interval-th row, beginning at start, which is drawn at random unless given; the number of rows drawn then follows from the interval and the size of the data. Give n instead to draw exactly n rows from a random start: the step is the number of rows walked divided by n, and need not be a whole number. With n_starts, several random starts are walked at a longer step, which gives the sample a design-unbiased variance. Given neither interval nor n, the design walks each stratum of design_stratified() as its within argument.

Usage

design_systematic(
  interval = NULL,
  start = NULL,
  order_by = NULL,
  na_rm = FALSE,
  n = NULL,
  n_starts = 1L
)

Arguments

interval

Sampling interval, a whole number of 1 or more: every interval-th row of the walk is taken. Give interval or n, not both. For a step that is not a whole number, give n.

start

Position in the walk of the first row taken, in 1:interval. The walk is the frame's rows in their order, or sorted by order_by when given, so with order_by a start of 3 takes the row with the third smallest value, not the frame's third row. Drawn at random from that range when NULL. A fixed start makes the design deterministic: each row is selected with probability 0 or 1, so inclusion_prob(), sampling_weight(), joint_prob(), draw(weights = TRUE), ht_total() and ht_mean() refuse it, while inclusion_prob(simulate = TRUE) reports those 0s and 1s. Not used with n or n_starts, whose starts are always random.

order_by

Optional column to sort by before walking the data. It changes which rows can appear together, so inclusion_prob() and joint_prob() compute against the sorted order too. Text is sorted byte by byte, as in the C locale, so the walk is the same in every session; ties keep frame order, so where the column has ties a seed is sure to draw the same rows only from a frame with its rows in the same order. Without ties the walk does not depend on frame order. One column: to walk by several, add a column of ranks built from them and give its name, as in the examples.

na_rm

When order_by is given, drop rows whose sort key is NA instead of raising an error.

n

Number of rows to draw, in place of interval. With N rows walked, each row covers a stretch of length n / N on a line from 0 to n, a start u is drawn uniformly from (0, 1), and the rows under u, u + 1, ..., u + n - 1 are taken. The step is N / n rows, every row has probability n / N, and the sample always holds n rows. When n divides N the probabilities are those of interval = N / n. A plan from plan_size() gives its n.

n_starts

Number of random starts, 1 by default. With n_starts = m and interval = k, m different starts are drawn from 1:(m * k) and each is walked at a step of m * k rows. Every row still has probability 1 / k, and the expected sample size is that of one start at interval. Each start gives a replicate, a systematic sample of its own, and two or more of them give a design-unbiased variance (see "Variance"). Needs interval, and a random start.

Value

A design object, for use with draw().

Variance

A systematic sample has a single random start. At a step of 2 rows or more, which is every interval above 1 and every n up to half the rows walked, neighbouring rows are never drawn together, so no design-unbiased variance estimator exists. ht_total() uses the successive-difference approximation (Wolter 2007), which compares neighbouring sampled rows in the order the design walked. With n above half the rows walked, every pair of rows can be drawn together (see joint_prob()), and ht_total() uses the same approximation. Sorting on a variable related to what you measure (order_by) is what makes systematic sampling efficient, and this estimator is the one that can see it; see ht_total() for its limits. When interval does not divide the number of rows walked, the sample size is random, and a term for that is added to the variance. A design given n has a fixed size and needs no such term.

With n_starts = m of 2 or more, the m starts are a simple random sample of the m * k possible ones, and each replicate r gives a total of its own, t_r, which is m times the sum of y / pi over its rows. The sample's total is their mean, and ht_total() uses the random group variance (Wolter 2007), (1 - 1 / k) * var(t_r) / m, on m - 1 degrees of freedom. It is design-unbiased whether or not m * k divides the rows walked, a replicate that drew no rows counting with a total of 0. as_svydesign() gives the same standard error with each replicate as a primary sampling unit, and refuses a sample with a replicate that drew no rows, which survey would leave out of its count of replicates. The price is precision: m starts spread the sample over the walk less evenly than one start at interval does, and few replicates give few degrees of freedom and a wide interval.

Within strata, as design_stratified(within = design_systematic()), each stratum has a start of its own and the variance is the sum of the strata's successive-difference approximations; see design_stratified().

References

Madow, W. G. and Madow, L. H. (1944). On the theory of systematic sampling, I. Annals of Mathematical Statistics, 15, 1–24.

Wolter, K. M. (2007). Introduction to Variance Estimation, 2nd ed. Springer.

See also

draw(), design_stratified()

Other designs: design_bootstrap(), design_certainty(), design_cluster(), design_multistage(), design_reservoir(), design_simple(), design_spatial(), design_spread(), design_stratified(), design_temporal(), design_weighted()

Examples

df <- data.frame(id = 1:100, value = (1:100) / 10,
                 site = rep(c("b", "a"), each = 50))
draw(df, design_systematic(interval = 10, start = 3))
#>    id value site
#> 1   3   0.3    b
#> 2  13   1.3    b
#> 3  23   2.3    b
#> 4  33   3.3    b
#> 5  43   4.3    b
#> 6  53   5.3    a
#> 7  63   6.3    a
#> 8  73   7.3    a
#> 9  83   8.3    a
#> 10 93   9.3    a
draw(df, design_systematic(interval = 25, order_by = "value"), seed = 1)
#>    id value site
#> 1  25   2.5    b
#> 2  50   5.0    b
#> 3  75   7.5    a
#> 4 100  10.0    a

# 30 rows from 100, a step of 3.33
draw(df, design_systematic(n = 30), seed = 1)$id
#>  [1]  1  5  8 11 15 18 21 25 28 31 35 38 41 45 48 51 55 58 61 65 68 71 75 78 81
#> [26] 85 88 91 95 98

# Four starts from 1:40, each walked at a step of 40: ten rows on
# average, as with one start, and a variance from the spread of the four
# replicates
s <- draw(df, design_systematic(interval = 10, n_starts = 4), seed = 1,
          weights = TRUE)
ht_total(s, "value")
#> Horvitz-Thompson total  (systematic design, n = 10)
#>   estimate 481
#>   se       18.99737  (analytic)
#>   95% CI  420.5419 to 541.4581  (t, 3 df)
#>   deff     0.0424  (better than simple random sampling)

# Walking by two columns: rank the rows by both, then walk the ranks
df$walk <- order(order(df$site, -df$value, method = "radix"))
draw(df, design_systematic(interval = 20, order_by = "walk"), seed = 1)
#>   id value site walk
#> 1 17   1.7    b   84
#> 2 37   3.7    b   64
#> 3 57   5.7    a   44
#> 4 77   7.7    a   24
#> 5 97   9.7    a    4
